title: Complex Ellipsis and Substitution
subtitle: Ellipsis (omitting words that are recoverable from context) and substitution (replacing repeated words with a short pro-form) make advanced English tighter and …
objectives: Understand and use: Ellipsis in reduced clauses — omitting a repeated subject, auxiliary, or verb when the meaning stays clear.

Understand and use: Omission patterns common in academic and literary writing — dropping relative pronouns and "that" in defining clauses, and omitting "which is/who is" before a reduced participle or adjective phrase.

Understand and use: Pro-forms in complex texts — using "do so," "one," "the same," "such," or simple auxiliaries to stand in for a whole verb phrase or idea already mentioned, avoiding repetition across sentences.

content.intro: Ellipsis (omitting words that are recoverable from context) and substitution (replacing repeated words with a short pro-form) make advanced English tighter and more natural, avoiding clumsy repetition.

rules.heading: a) Ellipsis in reduced clauses — omitting a repeated subject, auxiliary, or verb when the meaning stays clear.
rules.body:
• After "and/but/or" in parallel structures: She ordered coffee and [she ordered] a croissant.
  • In comparative/contrastive clauses: He works harder than she [works]. / Some like tea; others [like] coffee.
  • After auxiliaries, when the main verb is recoverable: He hasn't finished yet, but he will [finish] soon.
  • In subordinate clauses with the same subject as the main clause: While [he was] waiting, he read the newspaper.

rules.heading: b) Omission patterns common in academic and literary writing — dropping relative pronouns and "that" in defining clauses, and omitting "which is/who is" before a reduced participle or adjective phrase.
rules.body: The book [that] I mentioned is finally out. / The results, [which were] published last year, remain controversial.

rules.heading: c) Pro-forms in complex texts — using "do so," "one," "the same," "such," or simple auxiliaries to stand in for a whole verb phrase or idea already mentioned, avoiding repetition across sentences.
rules.body:
He asked her to leave, and she did so immediately. (= she left immediately)

If you need a pen, take one from my desk. (= a pen, not a specific one already mentioned)

The results confirmed the hypothesis; subsequent studies have done the same.

These devices are essential for sounding genuinely native-like: overusing full repetition, even when grammatically correct, sounds stilted at C2.

examples: She likes jazz, and her brother does too.
He hasn't called yet, but he probably will soon.
Some prefer working from home; others don't.
While waiting for the bus, she finished her book.
The report [that] we discussed yesterday has been revised.
The proposal, [which was] submitted last month, is still under review.
He asked me to stay quiet, and I did so, reluctantly.
If you need an umbrella, take one from the stand by the door.
The first study confirmed the theory; the second one did the same.
She can speak French fluently, and so can her sister.
He wanted to leave early, but couldn't.
Whatever the outcome, we'll accept it.

commonMistakes.wrong: She likes jazz, and her brother does it too.
commonMistakes.right: She likes jazz, and her brother does too. (or: ...and so does her brother.)
commonMistakes.why: "Does too" alone functions as the substitute verb phrase — adding "it" creates redundancy.

commonMistakes.wrong: He hasn't called yet, but he will do it soon.
commonMistakes.right: He hasn't called yet, but he will soon. / ...but he will do so soon.
commonMistakes.why: Use the bare auxiliary or "do so," not "will do it," which is redundant/informal here.

commonMistakes.wrong: While she was waiting, was reading a magazine.
commonMistakes.right: While waiting, she was reading a magazine. / While she was waiting, she was reading a magazine.
commonMistakes.why: If you omit the subject after "while," you must also omit "was" (ellipsis applies to subject + auxiliary together); otherwise, keep both.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you need a pen, take the one from my desk. (when no specific pen has been mentioned)
commonMistakes.right: If you need a pen, take one from my desk.
commonMistakes.why: "One" (indefinite substitution) is used for an unspecified item; "the one" implies a specific, previously identified item.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked her to apologize, and she did so it.
commonMistakes.right: He asked her to apologize, and she did so.
commonMistakes.why: "Did so" already replaces the whole verb phrase — don't add another object after it.

exercises.title: Gap-fill
exercises.instructions: Gap-fill (complete with the correct ellipsis/substitution or write "—" if a word should be omitted)

items.prompt: He plays the guitar, and his sister ___ too.
items.explanation: “Does too” substitutes for “plays the guitar too” — no need to repeat the verb phrase.

items.prompt: She hasn't finished the report, but she ___ by Friday.
items.explanation: The bare auxiliary “will” (or “will have finished”) stands in for the whole verb phrase, avoiding repetition.

items.prompt: ___ waiting for the results, they kept refreshing the page.
items.explanation: Omitting the subject and auxiliary after “while” (While [they were] waiting) is standard when the subject matches the main clause.

items.prompt: If you need a chair, grab ___ from the next room.
items.explanation: Indefinite “one” substitutes for an unspecified item (any chair, not a specific one).

items.prompt: The plan worked in the first city; it ___ in the second.
items.explanation: The bare auxiliary “did” (or “did so”) substitutes for “worked,” avoiding repetition.

items.prompt: He told them to wait, and they ___.
items.explanation: “Did” substitutes for the whole action (waited), already clear from context.

items.prompt: Some people love spicy food; ___ can't stand it.
items.explanation: “Others” substitutes for “other people” in this contrastive parallel structure.

items.prompt: The book ___ you recommended was excellent.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun “that/which” can be dropped entirely in a defining clause — that's what the em-dash marks.

exercises.title: Rewrite / Transformation
exercises.instructions: Rewrite / Transformation (rewrite each pair using ellipsis or substitution to avoid repetition)

items.prompt: My father can cook well. My mother can cook well too.
answer: My father can cook well, and so can my mother.
My father can cook well, and my mother can too.
items.explanation: “So can” (or “can too”) substitutes for the repeated verb phrase “can cook well.”

items.prompt: He hasn't decided yet, but he will decide soon.
answer: He hasn't decided yet, but he will soon.
items.explanation: The bare auxiliary “will” substitutes for “will decide,” avoiding repetition.

items.prompt: She was reading while she was waiting for the train.
answer: She was reading while waiting for the train.
items.explanation: Omitting the repeated subject + auxiliary (“she was”) after “while” tightens the sentence.

items.prompt: The first experiment succeeded. The second experiment succeeded too.
answer: The first experiment succeeded, and so did the second.
items.explanation: “So did” substitutes for the repeated verb phrase “succeeded.”

items.prompt: If you want a coffee, take a coffee from the machine.
answer: If you want a coffee, take one from the machine.
items.explanation: Indefinite “one” substitutes for “a coffee,” avoiding the repeated noun.

items.prompt: He told me to relax, and I relaxed.
answer: He told me to relax, and I did.
items.explanation: “Did” substitutes for the whole action (relaxed), already clear from context.

items.incorrect: She likes hiking, and her friend does it too.
answer: She likes hiking, and her friend does too.
items.explanation: “Does too” already functions as the substitute verb phrase — adding “it” creates redundancy.

items.incorrect: While she was cooking, was listening to music.
answer: While cooking, she was listening to music.
While she was cooking, she was listening to music.
items.explanation: If you omit the subject after “while,” you must also omit the auxiliary (“was”) — ellipsis applies to both together.

items.incorrect: He asked me to stop, and I did so it.
answer: He asked me to stop, and I did so.
items.explanation: “Did so” already replaces the whole verb phrase — don't add another object (“it”) after it.

items.incorrect: If you need a towel, take the one from the shelf. (no towel mentioned before)
answer: If you need a towel, take one from the shelf.
items.explanation: “One” (indefinite substitution) is for an unspecified item; “the one” implies something already identified.

items.incorrect: He hasn't replied yet, but he will do it tomorrow.
answer: He hasn't replied yet, but he will soon.
items.explanation: Use the bare auxiliary or “do so,” not “will do it,” which is redundant here.

items.incorrect: The first plan failed; the second plan did the same it.
answer: The first plan failed; the second did the same.
items.explanation: “Did the same” already replaces the whole action — don't add another object (“it”) after it.

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write two sentences about two people with a shared habit, using "does/did too" or "so does/did."
items.modelAnswer: My brother loves horror films, and so do I. My sister, on the other hand, does not.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a reduced clause after "while" or "when," omitting the repeated subject.
items.modelAnswer: When traveling alone, I always feel more observant of my surroundings.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using "do so" to substitute for a whole action already mentioned.
items.modelAnswer: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports early, and most people did so without complaint.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using indefinite "one" to substitute for an unspecified item.
items.modelAnswer: If you ever need a notebook, just grab one from the supply cabinet.

summary: a) Ellipsis in reduced clauses — omitting a repeated subject, auxiliary, or verb when the meaning stays clear.

b) Omission patterns common in academic and literary writing — dropping relative pronouns and "that" in defining clauses, and omitting "which is/who is" before a reduced participle or adjective phrase.
c) Pro-forms in complex texts — using "do so," "one," "the same," "such," or simple auxiliaries to stand in for a whole verb phrase or idea already mentioned, avoiding repetition across sentences.
